Bitcoin is a tool. It is money. That person who “loves it” is…

an unbanked child in a South African township. 

a single mom in the Philippines receiving Bitcoin from her sister in the U.S. and saving it.

the obnoxious, stereotypical “crypto bro” who holds it and is just trying to get rich quick.

the sound money libertarian who loathes government. 

a store owner in El Salvador who just accepts it as money, holds it, and really doesn’t think that much about it.

Is there a U.S. dollar culture? Is there a global financial system culture? Does gold have a culture? Does fire have a culture? Does electricity have a culture? Does the mobile phone have a culture? Does water have a culture? 

We assign this narrative of a “cultural value” to that which is proximal to us, that which captures our attention. It is a peculiar phenomenon of an emerging technology as it climbs its global adoption curve. This perceived cultural value morphs as our awareness of the spectrum of users and participants increases. And this cuts many ways. The chart gazer on Wall Street is just as unaware of the “cultural value” of Bitcoin in a South African township as the average shop keeper in that township is of the “cultural value” of Bitcoin to that Wall Street chart gazer and his/her peers. 

Books can, should and will be written about this evolving phenomenon. As they have been about other technologies. However, because Bitcoin is how the world will eventually store, represent, and exchange “value” there is a heightened premium to all of this. 

If you read this far and haven’t already done so, there’s no better time than now to start studying Bitcoin. Your future self will thank you. 🙏🧡
